To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the progress examination scores of the first four years of the PharmD program were strongly correlated to the cumulative GPA and national licensing exam scores.

the second year progress examination program strongly predicts failure to graduate on-time and failure to earn a GPA below a 3.0; and that the first year through fourth year progress examination programs identify students at risk for failing the national licensing examinations on their initial attempt.
the progress examination is an effective assessment of student failure to demonstrate competency and is a useful predictor of student performance on the national licensure examinations.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development, implementation, and evaluation of a progress examination program that accurately identifies students at risk of not graduating on time, failing to meet minimum GPA requirements, or failing the national licensing examinations.

the criterion-related validity of our progress examination program, which is a series of examinations administered to all pharmacy students in their first year through fourth year of the professional curriculum.

the development of the Progress Examination Program (PEP) at the University of North Carolina Eshelman School of Pharmacy (UNCESoP) to identify and remediate students who are failing to demonstrate competence in the PharmD curriculum.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the progress examination scores are a valid measure of student competence.
the progress examination scores are a valid predictor of student success on the national licensing examinations.
the progress examination accurately assesses student performance in the curriculum.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the examination program is a reliable predictor of students at risk for failing to demonstrate competence in the pharmacy curriculum.

the progress examinations are a valid assessment of students’ ability to demonstrate competence in the knowledge, skills, and attitudes required to practice pharmacy in a patient-centered environment.

our progress examination program accurately identifies student failure to demonstrate the requisite knowledge, skills, and attitudes for pharmacy practice and that this information is useful for identifying students who are at risk for academic failure.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the progress examination is a valid measure of student competence and should be used to identify at-risk students and provide appropriate remediation.
pharmacy schools should consider implementing a progress examination program to identify at risk students and provide remediation.
pharmacy schools can use progress examinations to predict student performance on national licensing exams.
